newsitem.title: USA: Sun Micro to buy Internet appliance startup Diba.
newsitem.headline: Sun Micro to buy Internet appliance startup Diba.

text.p: Sun Microsystems Inc. Thursday agreed to buy Diba Inc., a Silicon Valley startup which pioneered the concept of linking devices such as smart phones and televisions to the Internet.

The acquisition would give Sun Microsystems a boost in the race to develop simpler devices than personal computers for accessing information. These devices could include TV set-top boxes, car navigation systems and even kitchen appliances.
The value and terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Two brothers, Farzad and Farid Dibachi, founded Diba less than two years ago in Menlo Park, Calif. to design technology for making electronic components for a new generation of simple computers so-called Information Appliances.
Diba will become Sun's Consumer Technologies Group, a new business unit within its Sun Microelectronics division.

The effort will face competition from formidable rivals such software giant Microsoft Corp. and database leader Oracle Corp. Both have launched efforts around consumer products that compete with Diba.

In April Microsoft agreed to acquire WebTV Networks, a deal valued at $425 million which is awaiting regulatory approval, and in May a deal Oracle's Network Computer Inc. acquired Navio Communications Inc., from a group of investors which included Netscape Communications Corp..

Microsoft, whose Windows operating systems runs on more than 90 percent of personal computers, last year introduced its Windows CE system for small mobile devices, and Oracle has been pushing the concept of $500 Network Computer devices.
"It's a poker game ... this is a high stakes table," said Dataquest analyst Allen Weiner.
"All of these companies are chasing a vision which is going to to take at least five years to make any kind of significant inroad and penetration into consumers' houses."
Both Sun and Diba said the new Sun group will pursue Diba's goal of supplying technology to consumer electronics companies, rather than building the products themselves.

"From the very beginning our position was that one product wasn't going to make it, that there was going to be a multitude of products," said Diba President and Chief Executive Farzad Dibachi. "None of these products themselves are going to sell millions and millions of products. You've got to have a combination of products."
Chet Silvestri, president of Sun Microelectronics, said interactive digital TV set-top boxes are one obvious market, but various mobile devices also will be important.

The companies began talks about collaborating in March, and eventually Sun decided Diba's technology was key to its strategy for consumer products. Sun hopes to provide devices with "Web-tone" as reliable as telephone dialtone is today.
Silvestri said Diba's technology will be used with Sun's Java environment, and Sun is already working on integrating it into its microSPARC and Javachip semiconductor designs.
Analysts said after a conference call with executives that they believe the transaction involved stock-based incentives. One estimated the valuation at somewhere around $30 million.
Diba employs 79 people and had raised about $10 million from founders and from strategic investors Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Zenith Electronics Corp.
"We were actually on the verge of becoming profitable," said Dibachi. "The original concept was to go and get a big brother, and we decided just to go for the fatherly figure."
